claims.text: Large language models have a propensity to generate hallucinations, which are plausible, factually-incorrect responses expressed with striking confidence.
Hallucinations and other non-factual responses generated by LLMs can be detected by examining the uncertainty of the LLM in its response to the pertinent prompt.
Uncertainty quantification methods for LLMs apply across chatbot, textual, and embodied artificial intelligence applications in robotics.

evidence.description: integration of LLMs raises valid questions on their reliability and trustworthiness, given their propensity to generate hallucinations: plausible, factually-incorrect responses, which are expressed with striking confidence.
Previous work has shown that hallucinations and other non-factual responses generated by LLMs can be detected by examining the uncertainty of the LLM in its response to the pertinent prompt
Furthermore, we highlight applications of uncertainty quantification methods for LLMs, spanning chatbot and textual applications to embodied artificial intelligence applications in robotics.

methodologies.name: Taxonomic Survey of Uncertainty Quantification Methods
methodologies.description: A comprehensive systematic survey and taxonomy unifying existing uncertainty quantification methods for LLMs to evaluate their features, strengths, and weaknesses.

limitations.text: LLMs tend to generate hallucinations—plausible, factually-incorrect responses expressed with high confidence—which harms their reliability and trustworthiness.

future_work.text: Addressing open research challenges in the uncertainty quantification of LLMs.
